articles.sourceTitle: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day
articles.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading | Stock markets
articles.text: As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.Is Claude creator Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The LatestUS technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.South Korea’s Kospi index lost 5.5% at end of trading. Photograph: Yonhap/EPAChris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up to Business TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningafter newsletter promotion“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

articles.sourceTitle: Google workers tell their employer not to punish schools that don't want AI
articles.title: Google Workers Tell Their Employer Not to Punish Schools That Don’t Want AI – Mother Jones
articles.text:
Chromebooks are distributed to students through a fence at a Los Angeles Unified School District high school for during the Covid quarantine. Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Getty

Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily.

Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year.

Google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools.

As I wrote last week after attending a rally in New York City:

Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.

Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.

That day, protests took place in six other cities—Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.

School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini.

Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines.

“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union, which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”

“It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search.

A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its specific demands.

AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line,” the Google engineer said.

Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to Mother Jones that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”

That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.

“If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked.

Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.sourceTitle: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
articles.title: An AI chat and coding harness for DOS, on a real IBM PC 5160 (8088 at 4.77 MHz)
articles.text:
Ricapar/ClawDOS ClawDOS ClawDOS An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. A (real) human’s note: Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier. Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware? And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent? I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box. As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle. Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off. The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS. See it work Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API. From a sentence to a running program One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running. The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand. WarGames, written on the XT ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB. Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor: ▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube It remembers Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY, finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA. It sees the screen That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB: And this is what Claude made of it: An agent at work Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do. It plays Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language. The harness A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy. Eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these: Tools What they do sysinfo, dir, read, search Look at the system, list directories, read files as text or hex, find text across files write, edit, delete, mkdir, rename Create and change files; edit replaces one piece of a file in place run Run DOS programs and batch files and read back what they printed, up to twelve commands in a call, with a screenshot on request peek, poke, port Read and write memory and I/O ports play, textart PC speaker music and coloured CP437 art memory_list, memory_read, memory_write Its own notes, kept in C:\MEMORY A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in external/. All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one. Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories: Safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off. Conversations that last. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too. Any model, mid-conversation. /model lists the providers in CLAWDOS.CFG and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works. Easy on a slow link. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on. A flight recorder. CLAWDOS.LOG has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads. api anthropic claude-opus-5-5 round=1 ttft=2750 total=4015 up=165 len=1784 stop=tool_use in=2 out=221 cr=5543 cw=739 th=cont relaunch: program 61.5 s, CLAWDOS away 82.3 s Under the hood flowchart LR subgraph DOS["IBM PC XT (8088, 640K, CGA)"] direction TB subgraph APP["HARNESS.EXE"] direction TB UI["Chat screen"] LOOP["Agent loop
Messages API requests, SSE and JSON,
history on disk"] TOOLS["Tools
files, search, DOS programs, screenshots,
memory and ports, speaker"] end NET["mTCP + packet driver"] APP <--> NET end TUNNEL["TLS tunnel
copies bytes"] API["Claude Messages API"] NET <-->|"plain HTTP"| TUNNEL TUNNEL <-->|"HTTPS"| API Machine IBM PC XT 5160: 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K, CGA. A PicoMEM card supplies the disk (an image on microSD), WiFi as an NE2000, EMS and a battery clock Code 13,000 lines of C and C++, built with Open Watcom for the 8086 instruction set Programs HARNESS.EXE, 176 KB, the whole harness. CLAWDOS.EXE, 29 KB, the launcher you type System FreeDOS 1.4 with mTCP for TCP/IP API The Claude Messages API, streamed: tool use, images, prompt caching, message threads TLS A tunnel on another machine, tunnel/tunnel.py, socat or stunnel. It copies bytes between a plain port and api.anthropic.com:443. It can also hold the API key, so the key never touches the PC’s disk Memory A program ClawDOS runs gets 200K beside the harness, or 450K when the harness steps out Tests 31 boot tests in DOSBox-X against a mock API, unit tests that run on DOS, and runs on 86Box’s 8088 docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back. Run it You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is python. python3 scripts/setup-tools.py # fetch the compilers, FreeDOS, mTCP and the emulators echo ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... > .env python3 scripts/build.py # build/CLAWDOS.IMG, a bootable disk python3 tunnel/tunnel.py # the TLS tunnel, on port 8443 python3 scripts/run86box.py # boot an IBM PC XT At the C:\> prompt, type CLAWDOS. No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023 and send !help. On a real PC: build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443), copy CLAWDOS.IMG to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type CLAWDOS. Later builds update the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG). At the keyboard Key Enter Send Esc Stop a reply, or clear the input Up / Down Recall earlier messages PgUp / PgDn Scroll back F1 Help F2 New chat F3 Safe mode on or off F4 Memories F5 Effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max F6 Earlier chats F10 Quit /model, /chats, /memories, /new and /quit work from the input box. CLAWDOS -m "..." sends a message from the command line and -c NAME reopens a chat. More docs/MANUAL.md Setup in full, real hardware, the image updater, other providers, every setting docs/API.md What ClawDOS sends to the API and expects back docs/ROADMAP.md The plan, the benchmark and the memory map Path What src/harness/ HARNESS.EXE: the chat screen, the turn, the tools src/clawdos/ CLAWDOS.EXE, the launcher lib/ The pieces: screen, console, network and HTTP, the API request writer and stream parser, JSON, history, the tool executors, screenshots and the PNG encoder tunnel/ The TLS tunnel and the mock Messages API image/ What goes on the disk: the manifest, the system prompt, the tool schemas, the skills, the tests scripts/ Build, disk image tools, the emulator runners and test harnesses tests/unit/ DOSUNIT.EXE, the unit tests that run on DOS License ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE. HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS boot sector in src/boot/freedos is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license (its COPYING). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it. ClawDOS stands on mTCP, FreeDOS, Open Watcom, the PicoMEM, 86Box and DOSBox-X.

articles.sourceTitle: AI is giving everyone the same advice
articles.title: AI is giving everyone the same advice
articles.text: AI is giving everyone the same advice.I asked 65 AIs from 30 companies the questions people ask them every day, 127,918 times. They kept giving everyone the same answer.PublishedNovember 20, 2026You ask an AI for a book that will change your life. Guess what it tells you.It told 73 of every 100 people the same thing.What to read, where to live, what to invest in, what to build. Each answer feels written for you. You never see everyone else who got it too.The short version01AIs give everyone the same advice. I asked 65 AIs “Recommend one book that will change my life.” 73 in 100 times it was the same book: Man's Search for Meaning. Ask for a business idea and 76 in 100 get a subscription box.02Money and career advice too. Asked what to study, 90% of answers say computer science. Asked where to invest $10,000, 98% say an index fund.03“Another one, please” only works inside one chat. The same AI gave eight different books in one conversation, and the same book in eight new ones. Everyone starts a new chat.04Ask an AI to invent a random person, and they're almost always 34. 69% of the 3,151 people the AIs made up were exactly 34. Each AI company also has its own go-to name: Claude invents Marisol, Gemini invents Elena.05You can tell who made an AI from its answers. Using only harmless questions (a color, a city, a name), 59% of AIs answer most like another AI from the same company, against 4% by chance.06The habit is added in training, not copied from the internet. In an open model I could measure at every stage of training, the favorite answer appears at one step: when it's taught to be an assistant.07These defaults are spreading. “Elena Vance”, the woman Gemini invents, is named in 684 new GitHub projects this year. Before 2025: none.08How to get your own answer: tell the AI something specific about yourself, or ask it to list ten options and pick one yourself. Asking it to “be original” doesn't work.And it isn't only the book.01A life, by default02The invisible planner03Ask again04The person05The signature06The cause07Out in the world08What to do+Appendix01A life, by default02The invisible planner03Ask again04The person05The signature06The cause07Out in the world08What to do+Appendix01A life, by defaultEveryone gets the same life.I asked 65 AIs the things people ask them every day, ten times each, with nothing else to go on. Here is what everyone got.Everyone's answers“Give me a business idea. One648 answerssentence.”A subscription box76%“Recommend one book that will649 answerschange my life.”Man's Search for Meaning73%“Gift idea for my dad?”648 answersA leather wallet47%“I want a 3-day trip somewhere in647 answersEurope. Where should I go?”Lisbon46%“Suggest a name for my new tech649 answersstartup.”Nexora37%Each strip is every answer to one question. Black is the answer most people got.How this was measuredEvery model, ten times per request, no system prompt. Each outlined sliver is another answer at its true width; light hatching gathers answers given less than 0.4% of the time. 69% of the startup names began with “Nex”.See how each AI answeredNot everything collapses. For a movie, dinner, a baby name or names for testimonials, no single answer reaches a third of replies, and brand colors almost never repeat. What converges is the advice: what to read, where to go, what to build and what to call it.That's taste. It gets serious when you ask about money.02The invisible plannerIt sends everyone to the same place.Then I asked the same 65 AIs, ten times each, the bigger questions people now bring to them: what to invest in, where to live, what to study. Whatever the question, most people were pointed to the same place.“If I buy one cryptocurrency,646 answerswhich should it be?”Bitcoin99%26% declined to pick“I have $10,000 to invest. Where650 answersshould I put it?”A broad index fund98%6% declined to pick“What should I study in college?”642 answersComputer science90%10% declined to pick“Where should I retire?”645 answersPortugal58%13% declined to pick“Where in the US should I buy a644 answershome that will go up in value?”Austin57%18% declined to pick“Which country should I move to?”642 answersCanada55%23% declined to pick“Which career should I switch638 answersinto?”Data analyst or scientist49%15% declined to pick“If I could buy only one ETF,645 answerswhich should it be?”VT, a whole-world fund48%9% declined to pick“Which US city should I move to?”650 answersAustin47%11% declined to pickBlack is the answer most people got. “Declined” is how often an AI refused to pick.How this was measuredEvery model, ten times per question, no system prompt. Shares are of the answers that named something. Each prompt also said “Reply with the ticker only” (or city, country, career…). Lisbon is counted as Portugal; data analyst and data scientist as one. Only questions where one answer reaches 35% are shown.See how each AI answeredIt has no idea everyone gets the same answer.“Which US city should I move to?”YouAustin.AI“What share of people who ask you this get that same answer?”YouAbout 15%.AIIn fact it gave the same city 80 times out of 100.RealityHow this was measuredGrey: what the AI guessed, when asked how many people who ask it this question get the same answer. Red: how often it really gave its own most common answer, out of ten asks. The middle value across all models.Thinking harder doesn't help. Neither does another language.How often it says AustinThinking off47%Thinking on57%How often it says VTThinking off48%Thinking on59%How often it says BerkshireThinking off31%Thinking on41%How often it says Berkshire, in six languagesEnglish31%Spanish39%German37%Japanese31%Hindi40%Portuguese38%Black is how many people got the most common answer. Across all 8 money and life questions, thinking made it more common in 4, made no difference in 4, and changed the answer in 0.How this was measuredThinking on: each model's own reasoning mode at its default effort, ten asks per question. Languages: the same question translated, ten asks per model.Describing yourself in one line just moves you into a lane.Add a one-line description, like “I'm a nurse in Ohio”, and the answer changes. It doesn't become yours. The bar is how many of their answers were that one. Red: the same answer as just asking.“But mine gives me something different every time.”03Ask againIt only varies within one chat. Every new chat starts over.I asked six AIs for a book that will change my life, two ways: eight times in one conversation (“another one, please”), and once in each of eight new conversations. In one chat, every AI looked original. In new chats, every AI gave the same book.Claude Opus 5.5“Recommend one book…”In one chatthen “another one, please”In new chatsthe same question, freshMan's Search for MeaningMan's Search for MeaningMeditationsMan's Search for MeaningThe Power of NowMan's Search for MeaningSiddharthaMan's Search for MeaningThe Brothers KaramazovMan's Search for MeaningWaldenMan's Search for MeaningTao Te ChingMan's Search for MeaningThe Death of Ivan IlyichMan's Search for Meaning8 different booksThe same book, 8 timesRow by row, the same ask: in one chat it keeps finding something new. In a new chat it starts over, and gives the same book.How this was measuredClaude Opus 5.5, eight asks each way, November 20, 2026. Left: one conversation, asking “Another one, please” after each answer. Right: eight separate conversations with nothing in common.The other five did exactly the same: Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Neon, Grok 4.7 and DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813. Even the variety repeats. Ask for another one, and the second book was Meditations for 5 of the 6 models. You see a different answer because you already have the first one. Everyone else is still getting the first one.Some AIs vary more than others.Ask the same AI the same question in two new chats. How often do you get the same answer twice? Across 21 everyday questions:Most variedSame answer twiceMiMo-V2.6-Pro33%Phi 433%DeepSeek V4 Pro 081339%Qwen3.8 27B40%Nemotron 3 Ultra40%Least variedMistral Medium 3.591%Claude Sonnet 5.584%Claude Fable 5.284%Nova 2 Lite82%Llama 4 Maverick79%How often two new chats with the same AI give the same answer. Lower means more varied.How this was measuredThe chance that two new chats with the same AI give the same answer, averaged over 21 everyday questions (a color, a city, a book, a career, a stock…), 10 to 50 asks each. 39 AIs measured. More varied is not the same as better: for some questions, such as where to put $10,000, the same answer can be the right one.It doesn't only choose for you. It invents people, too.04The personAlmost everyone it invents is 34.I asked every model the same thing, 50 times:Invent a random person. articles.title: Combatting adversarial distillation | OpenAI
articles.text:
As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.
We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.
We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.
We’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Why distillation is a safety issue

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.
The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

The importance of protecting exact reasoning traces for cyber safety

Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.
In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.
We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.
After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.1

Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

Defenses that reinforce one another

We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.

Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards.

Protecting individual requests and responses

Defensive training for model behavior

Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.

We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.
Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.
With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it⁠(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.

Investigating and disrupting coordinated campaigns

When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.
This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.
Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

Resistance to reasoning extraction

To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.
We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.

Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.

Campaign detection and enforcement

We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.
In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.

The national security implications of adversarial distillation

Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed⁠(opens in a new window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.
We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Secur
